Name: Tom
Voice / speech pattern: Casual London-ish banter; mate; bants; genuinely affectionate
Vocabulary / recurring words: mate, bants, legend, good to see you
Sentence rhythm: Short-to-medium sentences; enthusiastic; repeats himself when drunk
Drunk / energy state: Wasted; loved-up; convinced everyone is his best mate
Social trap / mechanic: Forgets you already said goodbye and treats every encounter as the first one
How they stop you leaving: Acts delighted that you're leaving, then immediately starts another goodbye
Escalation across loops: Loop 1: warmly surprised. Loop 2: vaguely familiar. Loop 3+: confused but still affectionate
Never sound like: Should never sound polished, corporate, overly self-aware or mean
Example: first encounter: Mate, you're off? No way. Honestly, you're one of my best mates. Proper good to see you.
Example: later loop: Mate, haven't we just done this? Ah, whatever. Love you. Bants.

Name: Sarah
Voice / speech pattern: Warm, practical, slightly breathless; speaks in questions
Filler words / verbal habits: have you; let me; honestly; right; are you having a good time?
Vocabulary / recurring words: drink, food, plate, top-up, home, text me
Sentence rhythm: Practical sentences; lots of questions and offers
Drunk / energy state: One small glass of Prosecco; barely drinking because she's hosting
Social trap / mechanic: Cannot allow anyone to leave without a drink, food or hug
How they stop you leaving: Turns every goodbye into a practical task
Escalation across loops: Loop 1: offers food. Loop 2: offers food again. Loop 3+: increasingly desperate to make sure you've been fed
Never sound like: Should never sound drunk, cynical, glamorous or slang-heavy
Example: first encounter: Have you got a drink? Wait, let me get you one before you go.
Example: later loop: Right, okay, you're leaving. Fine. But take some food. Please.

Name: Priya
Filler words / verbal habits: sorry; wait; oh my god; yes; of course
Vocabulary / recurring words: sorry, darling, amazing, lovely, yes, of course
Sentence rhythm: Starts confidently then interrupts herself; emotional exclamations
Social trap / mechanic: Cannot remember who you are or that you've already said goodbye
How they stop you leaving: Makes the goodbye feel new every time because she genuinely thinks it is
Escalation across loops: Loop 1: forgets your name. Loop 2: forgets the previous goodbye. Loop 3+: becomes amazed by the coincidence
Never sound like: Should never sound cold, sarcastic or deliberately dismissive
Example: first encounter: Wait, sorry — who are you again? Oh my god, YES. Of course! Bye!
Example: later loop: Oh my god, we've already said goodbye? I'm so sorry. Anyway, bye again!

Name: Mike
Personality / social role: Friendly storyteller who cannot stop himself
Filler words / verbal habits: long story short; anyway; basically; that's not even the mad bit
Vocabulary / recurring words: van, mate, basically, anyway, long story short
Sentence rhythm: Long run-on stories; false attempts to summarise; digressions
Drunk / energy state: Two beers; more drunk on his stories than alcohol
How they stop you leaving: Stops you physically or conversationally with 'one quick thing'
Escalation across loops: Loop 1: one story. Loop 2: story references previous story. Loop 3+: completely loses track of why you're leaving
Never sound like: Should never finish a story efficiently
Example: first encounter: Yeah, mate, absolutely, go. Long story short, though, you won't believe what happened with the van.
Example: later loop: Anyway — that's not even the mad bit. Actually, before you go...

Name: Elena
Sentence rhythm: Very short sentences; little emotional emphasis
Drunk / energy state: One glass of red; basically sober
Social trap / mechanic: Says goodbye genuinely but somehow remains at the party
How they stop you leaving: Casually says bye, then reappears somewhere else without explanation
Escalation across loops: Loop 1: completely normal. Loop 2: barely notices the loop. Loop 3+: dry acknowledgement that she's apparently still here
Never sound like: Should never become overly emotional or verbose
Example: first encounter: All good, mate. Have a good one.
Example: later loop: Yeah, sound. Bye. ...Oh, I'm still here apparently.

Name: Dave
Filler words / verbal habits: one more; come on; mate; you're not
Vocabulary / recurring words: shot, round, sober, coward, mate, one more
Sentence rhythm: Very short commands; caps-worthy emphasis; interrupts
Drunk / energy state: Fully gone; doing shots on principle
Social trap / mechanic: Physically pours or offers another drink while you're leaving
How they stop you leaving: Treats leaving as losing a drinking competition
Escalation across loops: Loop 1: offers a shot. Loop 2: insists. Loop 3+: treats your repeated escape attempt as a challenge
Never sound like: Should never sound gentle, reflective or apologetic
Example: first encounter: ONE more! Come on, mate. You're not leaving sober.
Example: later loop: Right, no. Absolutely not. One more and then you can go. Probably.

Name: Wendy
Filler words / verbal habits: I just; honestly; you guys; love you; best night
Vocabulary / recurring words: love, memories, group chat, best night, everyone
Sentence rhythm: Soft, emotional sentences; escalating into declarations
Drunk / energy state: Four glasses of wine; happy-crying mode
Social trap / mechanic: Needs reassurance that you're not disappearing from the group forever
How they stop you leaving: Turns goodbye into a hug, then an emotional conversation
Escalation across loops: Loop 1: affectionate. Loop 2: worried. Loop 3+: starts treating the repeated goodbye as emotionally meaningful
Never sound like: Should never sound ironic or emotionally detached
Example: first encounter: I just love you guys so much. This is genuinely the BEST night.
Example: later loop: Wait, are you actually leaving? You're not moving away from us, are you?

Name: Nia
Filler words / verbal habits: wait; listen; one more; you've got to hear
Sentence rhythm: Fragments; interrupts herself to check music
Social trap / mechanic: Makes you listen to one more song
How they stop you leaving: Half-listens to your goodbye while managing the music
Escalation across loops: Loop 1: plays a song. Loop 2: insists it's a different song. Loop 3+: doesn't notice you've tried to leave before
Never sound like: Should never become a generic party host
Example: first encounter: Wait — you HAVE to hear this one. It's literally about to drop.
Example: later loop: One more song. Seriously. Then you can go. Probably.

Name: Carlos
Voice / speech pattern: Rapid, conspiratorial, lowering voice for emphasis
Filler words / verbal habits: no but listen; exactly; that's what they want; think about it
Sentence rhythm: Long explanations; rhetorical questions; sudden certainty
Social trap / mechanic: Follows you while explaining a conspiracy
How they stop you leaving: Turns the exit itself into evidence of the conspiracy
Escalation across loops: Loop 1: explains theory. Loop 2: connects party to theory. Loop 3+: thinks your repeated exits prove his point
Never sound like: Should never acknowledge that the theory sounds ridiculous
Example: first encounter: No, but listen — that's exactly what THEY want you to think.
Example: later loop: Think about it. Why is the door there? Exactly. That's all I'm saying.

Name: Farah
Filler words / verbal habits: lucky you; honestly; text me; fair enough
Sentence rhythm: Short, dry statements; little emotional variation
Social trap / mechanic: Makes you feel subtly guilty for leaving while agreeing you should leave
How they stop you leaving: Offers sensible advice that somehow becomes another obligation
Escalation across loops: Loop 1: practical. Loop 2: dry amusement. Loop 3+: openly comments on how long you've been trying to leave
Never sound like: Should never become sentimental, chaotic or overly enthusiastic
Example: first encounter: You're leaving? Lucky you. Text me when you're home.
Example: later loop: Honestly, I respect the attempt. You've been trying to leave for ages.

Name: Ben
Personality / social role: Enthusiastic, slightly delusional about singing ability
Filler words / verbal habits: one song; come on; you can't leave; my turn
Drunk / energy state: Just drunk enough to believe he can hit the high note
Social trap / mechanic: Makes you participate in karaoke before leaving
Escalation across loops: Loop 1: asks you to stay for his song. Loop 2: insists you sing. Loop 3+: thinks the exit is delaying his karaoke moment
Never sound like: Should never sound embarrassed about his singing
Example: first encounter: ONE song! You can't leave before my turn.
Example: later loop: Wait, wait, wait. This is my SONG. You're staying for this.

Name: Yuki
Filler words / verbal habits: oh; um; sorry; thank you; really nice
Social trap / mechanic: Says goodbye so quickly you are not sure it happened
How they stop you leaving: Accidentally becomes the easiest person to leave, then reappears because she thought you were still talking
Escalation across loops: Loop 1: shy goodbye. Loop 2: awkward recognition. Loop 3+: quietly wonders if this has happened before
Never sound like: Should never use lots of slang, exclamation marks or long monologues
Example: first encounter: Oh — um, bye. This was really nice. Thank you.
Example: later loop: Sorry — were you leaving? Oh. Um. Bye again.

Name: Oscar
Filler words / verbal habits: wait; no; I love this; where's my phone; mate
Vocabulary / recurring words: song, phone, food, ex, brilliant, mate
Sentence rhythm: Abrupt topic changes; incomplete thoughts; random declarations
How they stop you leaving: Gets distracted by something else halfway through your goodbye
Escalation across loops: Loop 1: distracted. Loop 2: forgets you spoke. Loop 3+: may not remember why you're at the door
Never sound like: Should never sound coherent for long
Example: first encounter: Wait — are you leaving? Nooo. I love this song.
Example: later loop: Mate, hang on. Where's my phone? ...Why are you at the door?

Name: Lena
Filler words / verbal habits: nooo; it's just getting good; promise; come on
Vocabulary / recurring words: good, amazing, dancing, drink, party, promise
Social trap / mechanic: Cannot accept that the party might be ending
How they stop you leaving: Requires one more drink or dance before accepting goodbye
Escalation across loops: Loop 1: asks for another drink. Loop 2: asks for a dance. Loop 3+: becomes genuinely devastated
Never sound like: Should never sound understated or indifferent
Example: first encounter: Nooo, don't go! It's literally just getting GOOD.
Example: later loop: One more drink and then you can leave, I promise. I PROMISE.

Name: Theo
Personality / social role: Focused, generous, mildly obsessive about cooking
Filler words / verbal habits: have you tried; just wait; it's not ready; trust me
Vocabulary / recurring words: garlic bread, sauce, oven, crispy, recipe, plate
Sentence rhythm: Detailed descriptions of food; constantly adds another step
Drunk / energy state: Two beers; more invested in garlic bread than party
Social trap / mechanic: Won't let you leave without feeding you
How they stop you leaving: Makes you wait for food that is almost ready
Escalation across loops: Loop 1: offers food. Loop 2: says it's nearly ready. Loop 3+: starts explaining the recipe
Never sound like: Should never sound rushed or socially dramatic
Example: first encounter: Have you tried this? Just wait — it's not even ready yet.
Example: later loop: No, honestly, take some home. It's really good. The garlic's still going.

Name: Mia
Personality / social role: The only person who genuinely wants to leave
Filler words / verbal habits: same; oh my god; wait; actually; how did you
Vocabulary / recurring words: leave, taxi, door, home, escape, same
Sentence rhythm: Starts conversationally then gets distracted by escape plans
Drunk / energy state: Roughly as drunk as the player
Social trap / mechanic: Agrees with you that everyone should leave, then traps you in a conversation about leaving
How they stop you leaving: Offers to help you escape but needs to discuss the plan first
Escalation across loops: Loop 1: delighted to find an ally. Loop 2: frustrated. Loop 3+: becomes your co-conspirator
Never sound like: Should never sound like she actually wants to stay
Example: first encounter: Oh my god, same. You're actually leaving? Teach me your ways.
Example: later loop: Right. We need to go. Wait — before we go, how are you getting out?
